items.title: Google refuse la demande de Trump de rebaptiser l’Atlantique « Océan Trump »
items.description: Donald Trump affirme avoir contacté personnellement Sundar Pichai, le patron de Google, pour lui proposer de donner son nom à l’océan Atlantique. Selon le président américain, le dirigeant du géant technologique aurait décliné sa demande, invoquant notamment la dimension internationale des océans. Donald Trump voulait voir son nom associé à l’un des plus grands océans du monde. Lors d’un meeting organisé mercredi 21 octobre en Caroline du Sud, le président américain a raconté avoir sollicité Sundar Pichai, le PDG de Google, afin de rebaptiser l’océan Atlantique, voire le Pacifique, en « Océan Trump ». Une proposition qui aurait reçu une réponse négative, selon le récit du dirigeant américain. L’idée avait été évoquée quelques jours plus tôt, lors d’un rassemblement républicain organisé le 10 octobre dans le Tennessee, à l’approche des élections de mi-mandat. Donald Trump semblait alors envisager de pousser plus loin sa politique de changement de noms géographiques. Devant ses partisans, Donald Trump a expliqué avoir directement demandé au patron de Google s’il pouvait procéder à ce changement de nom. Il a ensuite rapporté la réponse qu’il lui attribue : un refus, justifié par le caractère international des océans et le nombre de pays concernés. Selon la version racontée par le président américain, Sundar Pichai lui aurait fait comprendre que les océans représentaient un cas différent de celui du golfe du Mexique, compte tenu de leur portée géographique et diplomatique. Donald Trump a finalement semblé renoncer à son projet, demandant à son public s’il valait mieux conserver le nom d’océan Atlantique. Toutefois, Google n’a pas confirmé la véracité de cet échange lorsqu’il a été sollicité par Newsweek. Après le « Golfe d’Amérique », une nouvelle tentative Depuis son retour à la Maison-Blanche, Donald Trump a multiplié les initiatives visant à modifier certaines appellations géographiques. En janvier 2025, il avait signé un décret destiné à renommer le golfe du Mexique en « Golfe d’Amérique ». Google Maps avait ensuite adopté cette appellation pour les utilisateurs américains, tout en conservant une présentation différente dans d’autres pays. En France, par exemple, la carte affiche le nom « golfe du Mexique », accompagné de la mention « Golfe d’Amérique ». La tentative de rebaptiser l’Atlantique semble toutefois se heurter à des obstacles plus importants. Contrairement à une appellation utilisée dans un cadre national, un changement de nom concernant un océan partagé par de nombreux pays soulèverait des questions de reconnaissance internationale. The post Google refuse la demande de Trump de rebaptiser l’Atlantique « Océan Trump » appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: The DEI Language That’s Doing More Harm Than Good
items.description: Last week, Senator Edward Markey published a social-media post seeking interns for his Boston office. He wrote that “BIPOC, LGBTQ+, working class, veterans, and other underrepresented candidates with Massachusetts ties are encouraged to apply.” Outrage quickly followed: Critics treated the post not as a straightforward attempt to encourage diversity in job applications, but rather as a discriminatory signal that white men would be disadvantaged in hiring. The Manhattan Institute’s Christopher Rufo called the help-wanted ad an open violation of civil-rights law and urged a federal probe. The former Trump Justice Department appointee Theo Wold wrote that a goal of Democrats is to ensure that young white men “have no opportunities to find gainful employment.” One response to Markey stated, “If you are a young White man struggling financially, I understand your frustration with the Iran conflict and gas prices, but you must understand that this is the official hiring policy of the entire corporate world if democrats return to power.” Because X rewards inflammatory retorts more than intellectual rigor, these particular claims of racial grievance are easy for skeptics to dismiss as sensationalism. Urging certain groups to apply for a job is not proof of hiring discrimination against others. Some groups that Markey’s post mentioned, such as gay people, veterans, and the working class, include lots of white men. There is overwhelming evidence that the Democratic Party’s goal is not “no opportunities” for white men, and that corporations are not a left-identitarian monolith. Still, setting all falsehoods and exaggerations aside, Democratic elected officials have long been more likely than Republicans to favor policies that consider race and sex in employment decisions. These policies sometimes result in credible claims of discrimination against white and/or male candidates: Large nonprofits , major cities , multinational corporations, and prestigious law firms have all lost court cases involving employment discrimination against white people or men, or altered their employment practices under pressure from federal or state agencies that enforce civil-rights laws. Republicans generally treat such discrimination as a bigger problem than Democrats, even as most Americans—including a majority of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents— reject preferential treatment in hiring and promotions for favored groups. Populist-right partisans are probably correct that they have a political opportunity in going after any left-leaning political, academic, or business elites who push such policies. [ Read: Democrats can’t let go of racial preferences. ] The issue may prove especially potent for men in Generation Z. As recently as 2019, just a third of young men perceived some discrimination against men in America. In 2025, 51 percent of young men perceived it. Those feeling aggrieved by Markey’s words should bear in mind that, at 80, his views about race were formed before the civil-rights era. For most of his life, identity politics in Congress favored straight white men. Perhaps he still perceives that all groups other than white men need reassurance, and would be surprised that young white men today have any such need. (His office did not respond to my request for comment.) But older legislators need to grasp that efforts to diversify organizations, many of which focus on new hires, mean that Gen Z has a unique experience of the job market. Exposing white men in this cohort to language that seems to treat them differently from other groups is particularly unwise––they are especially primed to infer discriminatory intent whether or not it is being implied. Cheryl Kaiser, a psychology professor at the University of Washington, researches how “well-intentioned organizational diversity initiatives create unintended consequences.” She told me in an email that, although outreach to particular identity groups is distinct from restricting hiring to those groups, “the mere presence of a diversity signal, not the signal’s actual impact in hiring decisions, can increase White Americans’ concerns that they’ll face racism.” (In fact, several federal and state laws prohibit discrimination based on race, sex, or other protected characteristics—and these are laws that are intended to protect everyone, not just women or people of color.) In scholarship published in 2021, Kaiser and her co-authors found that “simply exposing White Americans to organizational diversity signals” increased their perception of a bias in hiring against white men. That perception occurred “even with clear evidence of White advantage within the organization, a less-qualified White candidate, or abundant promotion opportunities for all employees. Nor was it limited to people predisposed toward biased beliefs: the effect did not depend on participants’ endorsement of group-based hierarchy or their level of racial ingroup identification.” In another research paper, from 2015 , Kaiser and her co-authors found that the mere presence of pro-diversity signals “cause White male mock job applicants to experience cardiovascular stress as well as anticipate experiencing discrimination when applying for jobs at these companies.” Of course, the fact that people perceive discrimination does not mean they are actually being discriminated against. And if diversity language were effective in contributing to more equitable hiring outcomes, even while upsetting a few overly sensitive sorts, there would be a strong case for retaining it. But Kaiser believes that “the types of diversity signals that cause backlash often do very little to effectively diversify the workplace.” Research she published in 2020 found that “racial minority employees sometimes see organizational diversity signals as overstating real commitment, which is linked to feeling less able to fit in or thrive.” Often, then, diversity signals confound all assumptions: “They don’t produce the hiring outcomes critics fear, they don’t produce the trust or inclusion benefits supporters are aiming for, and yet they still trigger the perceptual backlash described above,” Kaiser told me. To meaningfully reduce resentment, grievance, and reactionary identitarianism among young white men, Democrats should adopt rhetoric that unambiguously clarifies a commitment to equal opportunity. Some may find this advice frustrating. For decades, the political right insisted that racial preferences were immoral and illegal, and that diversity efforts should be restricted to outreach . Now they’re treating mere outreach as proof of illegal discrimination. But as Kaiser’s research shows, diversity rhetoric can have unforeseen effects. White identitarians would exist even in a world without bias of any sort in recruitment or hiring––but using language that fuels white identity politics, as Markey’s language did, is political malpractice that’s bad for Americans of all races, no matter how well intentioned it might be. Even if one argues that diversity advocates shouldn’t have to change how they communicate in order to avoid backlash, the reality seems to be that they do. As is often the case in politics, social progress requires forging broad coalitions of people who often disagree. That requires an understanding of psychology, attentiveness to possible sensitivities, and, yes, even compromise. Outreach that values diversity and inclusion is still possible. In 2015, the social psychologist Wiebren Jansen and co-authors found that “including the cultural majority group in an organization’s diversity approach” can help white men with a high need to belong feel included, and can increase support within organizations for diversity efforts. Senator Elizabeth Warren’s approach to recruiting interns is a good example of inclusive language. Her call for applications uses familiar and simple language, describing her office as “an equal-opportunity employer” that does not discriminate based on “race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, national origin, age, genetic information, disability, or uniformed service.” Warren “encourages all individuals from all backgrounds to apply.” Whether you’re Black or white or trans or gay or working-class or a veteran, if you are wondering whether people like you belong, that approach leaves no ambiguity: You’re encouraged to apply. “All individuals” are.

items.title: Auto Hall accélère le développement de FOTON au Maroc avec le lancement du TUNLAND
items.description: Africa Motors, filiale du Groupe Auto Hall, inaugure un nouveau showroom FOTON à Casablanca et lance la gamme de pick-up TUNLAND sur le marché marocain. Cette double initiative s’inscrit dans une stratégie visant à renforcer l’offre de véhicules utilitaires, le réseau commercial et le service après-vente. Le Groupe Auto Hall franchit une nouvelle étape dans le développement de FOTON au Maroc. À travers sa filiale Africa Motors, le groupe a inauguré, jeudi 22 octobre 2026, un nouveau showroom de la marque à Casablanca et annoncé le lancement de la gamme de pick-up TUNLAND. Ces deux initiatives s’inscrivent dans la continuité du partenariat noué en 2021 entre Africa Motors et le constructeur chinois. L’objectif est de consolider la présence de FOTON sur le marché national des véhicules utilitaires et de proposer aux entreprises, artisans et autres professionnels des solutions adaptées à leurs besoins de transport. Une gamme élargie pour les professionnels Depuis son arrivée sur le marché marocain, FOTON a progressivement développé son offre autour de plusieurs segments. Celle-ci comprend les mini-trucks, avec les modèles TM Diesel, TM1 et Wonder, ainsi que les camions légers Aumark S de 3,5 et 8,5 tonnes. Le lancement du TUNLAND vient compléter ce portefeuille en renforçant la présence de la marque sur le segment des pick-up. La gamme propose différentes configurations, notamment en simple et double cabine, ainsi qu’une version diesel dotée d’une technologie hybride légère. Les véhicules sont conçus pour répondre à des usages variés, en associant capacités de transport, équipements de sécurité, fonctionnalité de l’habitacle et confort. Les prix du TUNLAND débutent à 195 000 DH TTC, selon la version et les conditions commerciales en vigueur. Cette offre cible notamment les artisans, les entreprises, les exploitants agricoles et les professionnels ayant besoin de véhicules polyvalents pour leurs activités quotidiennes. 2026, une année de structuration Pour Africa Motors, l’année 2026 marque une phase de consolidation du partenariat avec FOTON. L’ouverture du showroom de Casablanca, la mise en place d’une organisation dédiée à la marque et l’élargissement de la gamme doivent contribuer à renforcer son positionnement sur le marché marocain. Le groupe entend également améliorer progressivement son dispositif après-vente et la disponibilité des pièces de rechange, deux éléments importants pour les professionnels dont l’activité dépend de la continuité d’utilisation de leurs véhicules. « L’inauguration de ce nouveau showroom et le lancement de la gamme TUNLAND constituent deux étapes importantes dans le développement de FOTON au Maroc » , souligne Adil Benhida, directeur général du Pôle Camions, Bus et Engins spéciaux du Groupe Auto Hall. Le responsable précise que la stratégie vise à bâtir une marque capable de répondre aux attentes des professionnels grâce à une offre compétitive, une gamme adaptée au marché et la proximité du réseau Auto Hall. Cap sur l’accélération commerciale en 2027 Après cette phase de structuration, Africa Motors prévoit d’accélérer son développement commercial en 2027. Les priorités annoncées portent notamment sur les camions de petit et moyen tonnage, l’élargissement progressif de la gamme, le développement du réseau et la mise en place de solutions de financement attractives. Le réseau du Groupe Auto Hall constitue un levier central de cette stratégie, grâce à sa présence dans les principales régions du Royaume. Le groupe mise sur cette implantation pour renforcer la proximité commerciale, accompagner les clients dans l’entretien de leurs véhicules et améliorer l’accès aux pièces de rechange. Pour Nabil Bendada, directeur de la marque FOTON, le développement au Maroc repose sur une gamme complète et accessible, soutenue par une organisation commerciale et un service après-vente renforcés. FOTON, un constructeur spécialisé dans les véhicules utilitaires Fondé en 1996 dans le nord de Pékin, FOTON est un constructeur international spécialisé dans les véhicules utilitaires, notamment les camions, les utilitaires légers et les pick-up. Son partenariat avec Auto Hall s’inscrit dans sa stratégie de développement à l’international. Créée en 2015, Africa Motors est une filiale du Groupe Auto Hall chargée de développer des partenariats avec des constructeurs automobiles internationaux, notamment chinois. La société distribue plusieurs marques au Maroc et contribue à la stratégie de diversification du groupe. Avec l’ouverture du showroom de Casablanca et l’arrivée du TUNLAND, Auto Hall et FOTON entendent ainsi renforcer leur positionnement sur le marché marocain des véhicules utilitaires, en misant sur l’élargissement de l’offre et l’amélioration de l’accompagnement des professionnels. The post Auto Hall accélère le développement de FOTON au Maroc avec le lancement du TUNLAND appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Motor rider allegedly stabbed to death at Akame
items.description: A motor rider, identified as Lorlorne Kudah, believed to be in his late 20s, has allegedly been stabbed to death at Akame in the Ketu South Municipality of the Volta Region. The incident reportedly occurred at about 2100 hours on Thursday, at a new site near the One District, One Factory (1D1F) cassava processing factory. Assembly Member of the area, Winfred Kwabla Dakunya, told the Ghana News Agency (GNA) that the alleged suspect, identified as Kwame Tsali, believed to be in his 30s and a native of Lotakor, was yet to be apprehended. He said a woman connected to the incident, who was relatively new to the community, had reportedly informed the police that her husband was responsible for the alleged killing. Mr Dakunya said the suspect’s father and brother had confirmed that he left home with his motorbike but could not establish when he returned. He added that the motorbike was reportedly found parked in the suspect’s room after the incident. The circumstances surrounding the alleged killing remain unclear, and the suspect is reportedly on the run. Mr Dakunya appealed to residents of Akame and neighbouring communities to remain calm and allow the police to investigate the incident. He urged anyone with relevant information that could assist in locating the suspect to cooperate with the police. Police have since commenced investigations into the alleged murder after recovering the body for autopsy.

items.title: Garden City University, Prempeh College partner to address decline in business studies
items.description: Garden City University (GCU) has established a strategic partnership with Prempeh College to address the challenges facing Senior High School (SHS) business students as they transition to higher education. The initiative seeks to tackle a growing concern in the education sector, where some business students reportedly abandon the discipline when progressing from secondary to tertiary education. Through early academic interventions, career guidance and technology-driven learning initiatives, the partnership aims to strengthen students’ foundations and encourage more of them to pursue business-related programmes at the university level. The collaboration is expected to introduce academic clinics and career-modelling activities before students begin their university application processes. These interventions are intended to help students better understand business-related disciplines and prepare them for the demands of higher education. Speaking to a section of business students at Prempeh College about the factors contributing to the transition challenges, several students identified negative peer influence, alongside other socio-academic factors, as a major concern. The discussions highlighted the need for targeted interventions to help students make informed academic and career choices and maintain their interest in business studies as they progress through the education system. In an exclusive interview with Joy Learning TV, the Head of the Business Department at Prempeh College, Ms. Helena Akowuah, underscored the importance of the institutional partnership. She highlighted the factors contributing to students’ shift away from business-related disciplines and outlined the need for a collaborative approach to sustaining their interest in commerce and related fields. Adding a higher education perspective, the Director of Admissions at Garden City University, Shannan Akosua Magee, emphasised the importance of maintaining a balanced focus across academic disciplines, particularly business and economics. “We have done well by pushing our science students to another level, but it must be noted that business and economics form the backbone of our country,” Ms. Magee stated. “Many universities in Ghana are still experiencing a decline in business student intake. Through this partnership, GCU is actively working to demystify rigid business modules and prove to secondary students that accounting and management are exciting, high-tech, and globally viable paths.” Ms. Magee further indicated that the Vice-Chancellor of GCU, Professor Eric Kwasi Ofori, was enthusiastic about the initiative, particularly its emphasis on entrepreneurship and its potential to create opportunities with global relevance. The partnership reflects a broader effort to strengthen the link between secondary and tertiary education by equipping students with the academic preparation, career awareness and confidence needed to pursue business-related programmes. By engaging students before they make critical decisions about their future studies, GCU and Prempeh College hope to address some of the factors that discourage learners from pursuing business and economics at the university level.

items.title: Bunkpurugu chieftaincy dispute: Chief Justice orders transfer of case to Tamale over security fears
items.description: The Chief Justice has granted a request by defendants in the Bunkpurugu chieftaincy dispute to transfer their case from the High Court in Nalerigu to Tamale over security concerns. One of the defendants, Elijah Saan, told JoyNews that they feared for their lives if they travelled to Nalerigu to attend court. He said the defendants had received intelligence suggesting they could be killed if they appeared in court in Nalerigu and had instructed their lawyer to apply for the transfer of the case to Tamale. The case was scheduled for hearing on Friday, October 23, 2026. However, the Registrar of the Nalerigu High Court confirmed to JoyNews on Friday that the Chief Justice had granted the request. The transfer comes amid heightened tensions in Bunkpurugu following the disputed enskinment of Melchizedek Musah Jamung as chief on September 14, 2026. The installation, which took place amid an ongoing chieftaincy dispute, reportedly triggered violence that left a woman dead and four others injured. Police have since been searching for the rival chief and other members of the Jamong royal family in connection with the disputed enskinment. The development has also prompted the Overlord of the Mamprugu Traditional Area, Naa Bohagu Abdulai Mahami Sheriga, to file an application at the High Court in Nalerigu seeking to have four people committed for contempt of court over the installation. In the application filed on October 14, 2026, the Nayiri accused the respondents of defying judicial processes by proceeding with the enskinment despite an ongoing legal dispute over the Bunkpurugu skin. The dispute between the Jamong and Jafouk royal families has contributed to persistent tensions in the area, with reports of farm destruction, arson and residents fleeing their homes amid fears of further violence.

items.title: [Rediffusion] Enfants vulnérables à Gaya : quelles réponses de protection ?
items.description: Listen to « Enfants vulnerables a Gaya : quelles reponses de protection ?(Forum) » on Spreaker. Ville frontaliere et important carrefour commercial, Gaya offre de nombreuses opportunites economiques. Cette position strategique expose toutefois les enfants a plusieurs risques, notamment le travail des enfants, la mendicite, la descolarisation, les violences, l'exploitation, la traite ainsi que les deplacements transfrontaliers non encadres. Au cours de cette emission, nous analyserons les principaux defis lies a la protection de l'enfance, les actions deja entreprises, les difficultes rencontrees sur le terrain et les solutions a envisager. Pour en debattre, nous recevons des acteurs engages dans la protection des enfants.

items.title: The Armageddon Economy
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube It can feel like an existential moment right now—one where many tech leaders are both warning against and accelerating the destructive forces of AI. But Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor argue that this could also be a turning point toward building something better. The authors of End Times Fascism talk with Galaxy Brain host Charlie Warzel about runaway wealth, the politics of AI, and how to prepare if the tech-bloated market crashes. The following is a transcript of the episode: Astra Taylor: You know, are there ways to deal with a crash that lets the people who’ve perpetrated this, like, eat the downside. Like, could this be an opportunity to get rid of some of the excess wealth and the inequality in this moment? Charlie Warzel: I’m Charlie Warzel, and this is Galaxy Brain . There’s all kinds of chaos in the world. There’s multiple wars. The ongoing climate crisis. It is a bizarre and existential moment. And Silicon Valley is not helping. AI researchers are quitting in droves, and they’re worried that what they’re building might kill us all. It’s easy, in this moment, to dismiss all of this talk reflexively—to see this as little more than a form of tech marketing. Or conversely, it’s easy to believe it all uncritically. But my guests today have a different framework from which to process this moment, both in Silicon Valley and in the rest of the world. In their new book, End Times Fascism , the writers Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor offer up an idea that what we’ve seen from tech leaders in the last decade—from the AI build-out to the tech leaders’ pivot to supporting and working with Donald Trump—is all part of a broader movement of politicians and titans of industry trying to consolidate power in a moment of global instability. That this movement is, in meaningful ways, circular. For example, the tech tools create the conditions for chaos, and then those same leaders capitalize on the chaos. Klein is a New York Times best-selling author and a professor of climate justice who has been interrogating corporate power for decades. Astra Taylor is a writer, documentary filmmaker, and an activist. Together their argument is an attempt to explain a theory of power here in this turbulent decade, and how it builds off of and is different from the previous eras. But I really wanted to bring them on to zero in specifically on the “end times” part of their argument. Because whatever you think about what’s going on with our tech leaders, it seems very clear that the industry has adopted a zealous, and even religious, attitude in recent years. Promises of both utopian salvation and apocalyptic destruction are now commonplace. Silicon Valley is currently enamored with and terrified by the prospect that they are building God. They’re asking the rest of us to have faith: to put our trust in the technology and in them. But what world are they really trying to build here? And how did we get here? Klein and Taylor join me now to talk about it all. Naomi Klein, Astra Taylor: Welcome to Galaxy Brain . Astra Taylor: Glad to be here. Naomi Klein: Thank you. Warzel: So I wanna just start straight off with definitions here. The book is called End Times Fascism . Let’s start with defining end-times fascism and also how it both iterates on and is different from previous forms of fascism. Taylor: We subscribe to a view of fascism as something that didn’t just emerge as a kind of rupture in Europe in the 20th century, but something as a through line. Fascism has precedence. So fascism is a form of far-right reactionary politics that uses democracy against itself, that creates kind of vertical alliances between corporate and political elites. It is an elite-led right-wing movement, and creates kind of solidarities with a group—classes of people we describe as the “injured powerful.” And so end-times fascism is our term for a form of fascism that is in dialogue, that is responsive to novel planetary-scale crises. So Hitler and Mussolini did not know a world with atomic weapons. That’s something that changes the nature of what it means to be human—the fact that we can cause that kind of annihilation. Wealth is extremely concentrated. It was concentrated then, but now is even more kind of globally connected and concentrated in the hands of single individuals, like someone like Elon Musk, the world’s first trillionaire. We also live in a world that is being destabilized by climate change. So, you know, the fascists of yore understood pollution in the sense of something localized, but they didn’t understand the way we’re altering the chemistry of the planet. That is a huge factor in our analysis, and of course now. All these threats are being compounded by artificial intelligence. And today’s fascists are responding to these very real risks by basically accelerating, by slamming their foot on the gas and basically deciding that they’ll protect their in-group, and believing that they’ll be safe no matter what. So that’s why we see, you know, all of these high-tech lavish bunkers and this drive to fortress the nation. So fascism is always a response to real crises. It’s always a response to threats from the left, threats of redistribution. But the nature of the threats that we’re facing have changed. And we have all changed, I think, in response to these crises. Warzel: Well Naomi, then maybe this is a moment to ask: Is there a distinction here between an opportunism—with taking some of these global crises, and, you know, you’re saying the reactionary nature is in response to that. Is it opportunism? Or is it trying to continue, in your minds, perpetuating that—because it is also very helpful to, you know, the causes of an oligarchical class? Klein: So fascism is always an alliance. This is something else that recurs through the history of fascism. The Latin word means “bundle”— fascia , right? So it always has these distinct elements. And the elements of the fascist bundle that we look at in the book—that we identify as being part of the far-right coalition that we’re writing about—include people who have a very literalist end-times religious belief, right? So they really do believe that we are entering the end of days. And we also look at people we’re calling “tech end-timers,” right? Who are very focused on AI, and they have a story that really echoes these religious stories about how a new age is going to begin, change absolutely everything. Maybe birth a new species. Summoning a god. Like, there’s a religious quality to the stories that some of the people at the forefront of AI are telling. And then we look at the mass ethno-nationalist base of the far right around the world. Not just in the United States, for whom the chosenness is citizenship, and the bunker is the nation-state. But only certain people get to stay. And they’re very focused on keeping people out, right? So in terms of whether it’s opportunistic or accelerationist, it depends on who we’re talking about. I think that for the religious members of this coalition, you know, some of it is just identifying the crises that Astra mentioned. Interpreting them as signs, right? As we face real ecological boundaries, lots of things that are accelerating pandemics are welcomed and interpreted as signs. But as this kind of millenarian fever takes hold, and there is this feeling among Messianic Jews and Christian Zionists that we really have entered the end of days. Then you get into a loop where—because you believe that the end times are upon us—you do accelerationist things, like you actively expect. Expand wars, right? So it isn’t just opportunistic; it isn’t just kind of like these things are happening anyway. It’s: Hey, let’s attack Iran; let’s expand the war to the whole region. All of this is good. The worse the better. Right? And this is the danger of this kind of religion—is that it interprets things that really are objectively bad as good, and has a built-in incentive to accelerate them. Not true of everybody who is Christian; not true of everybody who is Jewish. But it’s true of people who are the most kind of fundamentalist believers of this—these end-times prophecies. Then you have in the tech world, definitely you have opportunism. You know, we quote this now kind of famous correspondence between Peter Thiel and Jeffrey Epstein about: Okay, Brexit has happened; the U.K. economy is going down; it’s the era of collapse. You know, now it’s all about making money on the collapse, right? Return to tribalism. This is Epstein writing, right? And so I think that we are seeing a kind of Armageddon economy. You know, when I wrote The Shock Doctrine I wrote about disaster capitalism. This was more about taking advantage of punctuated shocks, right—like a war or a natural disaster. I think there is an economic shift going on now, where a lot of people are betting on bad times. Right? They are looking at the same forecast that we are, but they aren’t interested in thinking about how you mitigate them. They’re thinking: Okay, things are going down, but that doesn’t mean that we have to stop profiting. There’s money to be made in containing refugees. There’s money to be made in building prisons. And deportation flights. And mass surveillance. So it’s a pretty bleak economy. But it creates, once again, these negative incentives, right? Because once you’ve really invested in it, then you don’t want there to be good times, because good times are “bad.” And you know, we quote [Palantir CEO] Alexander Karp saying: “Bad times are good for Palantir, and that’s not good for the rest of us.” You know: We don’t want large parts of our economy that are very invested in these end times staying “bad .” Warzel: For this conversation, I wanna focus on that tech portion of your book. And I think you were speaking about the religious leaders, and the way that when you believe that you are in this end-times moment, this apocalyptic moment—you do accelerationist things. And I think, you know, when we’re talking about AI and the tech world as it is right now, a lot of people think—and you all write about AI as the creation of this, you know, godlike-superintelligence thing. Or whatever it is, right? Klein: Well, we quote them saying it. We don’t believe it. Warzel: Yes, you quote them saying that. But I also think, too, that the entire technology is in itself—it’s not just religious in what it could do, but it’s the entire technology is a faith-based technology. In the sense that you are always shadowboxing the future version of what this will be, right? The classic line is: This is the worst that technology will ever be. Just wait, just wait, just wait. And this idea that you are never selling anything that you currently have—you are selling the idea. And the way that sort of religious nature exists now, as the main form of marketing in the industry. As the main way that venture capital flows in. And that people, you know, gain a foothold in the industry and power. And so I think that is really interesting—the way that there is that parallel there. That the tech industry has sort of taken on a religious nature in just how it behaves. Taylor: Mm. Klein: Yes. Taylor: Yeah. I mean, and there was precedent for this. In the sense, I mean—if you go back to the old days, before they all came out as far right, I mean, we talked about the cult of the founder, right? I mean, they were described in the press as oracles, as prophets, right? They would be, like, pitching a delivery app, and people were like: You know, they’re bringing democracy. They’re bringing deliverance. And so that was part of their brand. And I think like any cult, when the evidence starts piling up against you, you dig in all the more. So I think your description of it as a “faith-based technology” feels really apt, right? It’s just like: Just believe; just put all the money in there. Just put all the resources in there. You know: Don’t doubt what we’re making. So, I don’t know. I mean, I think the lesson maybe here is as simple as “don’t worship capitalists,” right? Klein: But I think the imminence point is really key. Because, I mean—there’s always an imminence in capitalism. Where it’s just kind of always about to get better. The “trickle down” is going to happen. Like—just sort of pray to those gods, right? But there were still actual material products that were legible; that were kind of delivering the things that they said that they were going to deliver. And that people were paying money for. So I don’t think we have ever had as much of the global economy based on a bet of something that is supposedly about to happen—but that doesn’t line up at all with the product that is actually being sold. Right? So that sort of sense of living in the “about to,” living in the imminence: I don’t think we’ve ever been sort of not where we are, but in the about to be. And that does feel quite religious. Warzel: And there’s an odd dynamic to all of this, as well. As you mentioned the economics of the AI boom and everything being built toward this speculative future. But there’s also now—because of the amount of investment, because of how predicated the economy is on Nvidia and the Magnificent Seven stocks—there is also this apocalyptic quality to all of this. Where if the music stops, if the investment stops coming in, right, then you have this specter of an absolute bubble burst. A huge, 2008-style crash, taking everything with it. On the other side of it, there is this “We are fulfilling the promise of this investment.” And then there is all kinds of economic upheaval. And you know, rewriting the social contract, and all the things that these people are talking about. Which are in their own sense very apocalyptic, as they are so disruptive. And so it feels like no matter where you are, you’re boxed in at least narratively—with this idea that something massive is going to happen. Taylor: Yeah. Klein: Yeah. Well, and it’s not our imagination. I mean, we are being conscripted into this dream whether we like it or not. The way the SpaceX IPO was structured, right? Where just like—rather than having a wait period before the stock is in everybody’s pension who has a pension, right, they change the rules. So you have no choice but to be part of this massive gamble, right? That is all based on this extraordinary claim that in the future, this nonprofitable part of the company, the AI division, will eventually have a market worth $28 trillion. It’s just wild, right? Warzel: I’m curious: In your minds, what is the world that the tech right is trying to build? As in this whole group investing in all these different technologies. You know, from the things that Musk is doing to things that Palantir are doing. Like, what is the world that you see them trying to build right now? Klein: I think that there are different visions, and then there are hedges to those visions. And some of those hedges might be: Well, if this all goes down we’re gonna just go to our corporate city-state in Honduras. And if that doesn’t work, we’ll go to our bunker in New Zealand. Or if that doesn’t work, we’ll go to the one in Argentina. And maybe we’ll also build a space colony. Like there’s a lot of different stories being told. I don’t think there’s one coherent, like: “This is our Eden.” So they need bunkers to protect themselves if this all goes very wrong. I don’t think that the kind of bunkers are their utopia. I think the utopia, really, is one of dematerialization, if that resonates at all. Like, I think that this idea of kind of being free from the material world—and I think this is actually the most religious part of it—is that the whole story of modern capitalism has been about leaving as much of the physical world behind, and with its obligations, as you possibly can. So first, companies declare: Well, we’re not actually making products; we’re making brands. And other people can make the products. Right? But then it’s like—even that, you know: We’re not publishers; we’re just platforms. So we want the profits, but we don’t want the responsibilities. And AI is the ultimate version of this. Where you actually kind of can upload your consciousness. You can live forever; you are free of the physical world, and you’re just betting on a machine world. So if there is a utopia, I think it’s being free of workers, infrastructure. Like, they don’t want to own their own data centers. I think they want to float upwards. Warzel: In your guys’ estimation, has this always been the project? Because for some, it seems yes, right? You have the Peter Thiels—always been reactionary, even early on questioning democracy as a useful concept to him and other people. Musk has been obsessed with transhumanism. But there’s also a lot of people who, I would argue, have come into this kind of bumbling, right? Like, they just wanted to build social networks or apps. Or, you know, make a website to rank who’s hotter in their dorm, and kind of stumbling into these roles as these new titans of technology and industry. And there was this liberal bent in Silicon Valley for a while, or at least a seemingly liberal facade in Silicon Valley. Does that feel like opportunism to you all, in the recent rightward pivot that a lot of these tech founders have had? Or do you think that there is something inherent in the project that you said—of sort of leaving the material world behind, being fully in the cloud, as it were—that would make it so that it was always going to lead to where we are now? Taylor: So I think we would argue that different conditions bring out different responses, different potentialities in people, different facets of them. I mean, I don’t think we should underplay how strong a right-wing bent there was in Silicon Valley. I mean, scholars have written about cyber-libertarianism and the kind of, you know, right-wing politics. So yes, you know: socially liberal but economically conservative. Or sometimes, in the case of Peter Thiel and his friends, just overtly reactionary and antidemocratic. So those ideas have been there, but they were tempered by the political and economic conditions. So I mean, I think there was a period when they’re building social media; they’re promising to democratize our culture and, you know, make the world a better place, where they could justify their extreme wealth. In terms of meritocracy, right? It still kind of fits in that paradigm. Like: We’re the smartest guys in the room. We’re the founders, and you all should bow down to us. But, you know, they were still kind of saying there would be these socially beneficial effects. In around 2014, 2015, when a “tech lash” started growing on the left or the right, that was challenged, right? I mean, so we argue that fascism, again, is always a response to crisis and a response to threats of redistribution. A threat from the left. And the tech lash was really pivotal. I mean, workers started organizing at these companies and demanding unions, and Me Too happened. And that was a very active force in Silicon Valley. Workers were saying: We want stronger environmental protections. Cities were saying: We don’t want your AI city. We don’t want sidewalk labs. Right? Countries were saying: We want privacy protections. Like, modest privacy protections would be nice. Right? Klein: The European Union. Taylor: Right. And so it was an affront to these guys and to their sense of themselves, but also to their business model. And I think they knew, rationally, that rolling out AI would be even more difficult, right? That it would receive even more of a pushback. Because most people are not clamoring for technology that threatens to take all the jobs, fill the internet with slop, possibly cause, you know, delusions in their friends and family members and children. And so they knew this. And they were already losing popularity. So I think these guys in that sense, you know—it’s a time for using the power they had amassed, right? And you know, we detail in the book why we think that they went in so hard with Donald Trump. And ultimately, we think it’s because of the material choice before them. They wanted to roll out AI without regulations. You know, with whatever energy they could get their hands on. They understood that to Trump, he’d love that it was gonna burn a lot of fossil fuels and boost the economy. And so they made a conscious deal. Warzel: So this case, that this rightward pivot has so much to do with the material needs of the tech companies responding to the AI build-out. What they need—both the lack of regulation, but also having, you know, friendly people like David Sacks. Who is a Silicon Valley insider who becomes the AI and crypto czar in the Trump administration for a while. You argue that, and it’s— Klein: I think he still has a lot of power in this administration, though he doesn’t have that position anymore. Warzel: Yeah; I mean, he just had dinner with a bunch of the AI executives as they’re talking about trying to “pace the frontier.” He’s definitely still in that mix. But there’s also this side of, you know, the founder psychology; as you said, the tech lash being this big part of it. How much do you weigh that? Taylor: Mm-hmm. Klein: Tech lash intersecting with AI, right? And this doesn’t start with ChatGPT, as you know, right? Like I wrote a piece about [former Google CEO] Eric Schmidt and the way he was pushing AI during the pandemic. First of all: The pandemic was very profitable for these tech companies, right? Because we’re all at home on our screens. Those of us who were not, you know, frontline workers. Right. Warzel: The Zoom revolution, yeah. Taylor: The Zoom boom. Klein: And it was the Zoom boom, and they all like—didn’t they double their wealth in the first two years? The billionaires and the tech billionaires? And the data-center build-out was frenetic in that period, right? Because so much streaming was happening; so much gaming was happening. And Eric Schmidt went on this big push of like: Isn’t Zoom school great? Isn’t telehealth great? Isn’t it like, maybe we should be more like China? And he made all these presentations in Washington about how the biggest problem with the U.S. in winning the AI race with China was all of these pesky privacy protections. Like, protecting people’s health records. And the fact that people didn’t want their kids under surveillance, and the fact that they didn’t want smart cities. And the whole frame was like: China is able to do all of this, because they have no privacy protections. And boo-hoo, the U.S. does, and the European Union is placing even more. Right? And so we see this moment that we’re in and the alignment with Trump as a revolt of the elites against regulation, and a very strategic alignment with someone who was sociopathic enough to let them do it, right? Because Trump’s relationship to AI and any other existential risk is just like: We all die sooner or later, you know? Warzel: You know, if you simply list off what AI is as a technology, and its promises, there’s something that I think ends up being pretty striking. Right? You have a technology that is trained on the ill-gotten, mostly, output of most of humanity. Requiring these material economic investments that are essentially unprecedented, and would yield unprecedented wealth and disruption, as we’re saying. And then this arguably quite false idea of creating perfect automated efficiency in markets and workplaces—such that humans aren’t really needed at all, right? And in that sense, it feels very end-timesy to me. Not in the sense that it will bring about the apocalypse per se, but in that there’s really nothing left for capitalism to do if it succeeds. And so my question to you: Is AI the final boss of capitalism? Is there anything left after it? Taylor: I mean, that’s interesting. You know, other people have phrased this like: So are these guys saying that AI is actually gonna bring about communism? Right? Like that’s the end point, because it’s, you know, sustainable super-abundance or whatever. Like, in this future you’ll never have to work again, and it’ll be leisure for all. So I mean, you know: I think the answer is no. Because their vision is not gonna come true as they are describing it, right? I mean, one of the recurring motifs of our book is that a group’s apocalyptic fantasies don’t have to be literally true. Or rarely are; never literally true. But they can cause a lot of havoc and a lot of damage regardless. Warzel: Right. Taylor: So I think they’re going to cause a lot of harm as they chase this vision. But there’s all sorts of questions that their end goal raises, right? Which is like: Yeah, how does capitalism work if people don’t have jobs and don’t have money? Like, okay—so you’re talking about a no-consumer future? It obviously gets to the point where they haven’t really thought this out. They’re just in the race, and they’re fine if they’re racing us off a cliff. And, in fact, the market seems to be catching up, right—with all the recent headlines about the fact that so much of this AI debt is actually now distressed, and the whole house of cards appears to be wobbling. Klein: And this is where I think their various escape plans do bear some attention. Because I think that there is this way that this is just all a massive gamble—and they do know it. Like, whether they know that it’s all going down or just part of it. I’m not gonna guess there. But I do think that all the hedges—and all the ways in which they have Plan Bs and Cs, right—is like if this goes down. You know, if say SpaceX valuation just seems to be fictional, seems to be notional, right? Like, I mean, and laughable. And everybody is just agreeing to go in it. Warzel: It’s about extending the light of consciousness throughout the universe. That’s like in the prospectus. It’s truly an actual dream. Like it is a fan-fiction scenario. Taylor: Yeah. Klein: Right. But I guess we’re pretty focused on what happens when this does pop, right? Whether it all goes down or partly goes down. What if their whole business model has been built on theft—Astra has called it “theft tech,” which I actually think is a very good phrase to describe a lot of AI—what are we owed before they get paid back? And how do we structure—like, how do we make sure that they aren’t able to just leave us with all the distressed assets? Where a few ultra-rich people pull off what in the book we call the “wealth rapture.” Right? Where they just ascend to their gated cities of various kinds and are like: Sorry, suckers . Because I do think that’s one of the futures that we’re looking at. And I think that they’ve structured their companies in a lot of cases where their personal wealth will be okay. And they do have various escape plans, and the rest of us get stuck with all of the risk of this. And we just have to have our eyes open about it. Warzel: You mentioned a couple—that’s one of the scenarios you’re looking at if this goes sideways. What are some of the other ones that you’re thinking about? Taylor: I mean, I think that we saw this with the recent Axios reporting that the heads of these companies are doing these disaster-scenario plannings. Right? They’re like: What if there’s a massive cyberattack that uses our agents, and then the public gets really mad at us? So the “disaster” for them—I mean, this is also a tell. The disaster for them is less the potential catastrophe—the cyberattack, the critical infrastructure going down—than the public’s response. And the fact that it could be a PR disaster for them in a moment of democratic leverage. So I think, you know, we should hedge too, and we should prep too. Like, we don’t know exactly what the unraveling of this bubble in this sector will be, right? Even the term crash implies something going down—like the sort of 1929 stock-market vision. And it doesn’t actually necessarily have to unfold like that. So there could be, you know, financial collapse of some kind of the sector. Or there could be some sort of disaster. So you mentioned the 2007 bailout. I mean, the thing about that is—you know, the money in that crisis was much more systemic. In the sense that it was banks and people’s literal homes, right? I mean so much of the capital involved. There’s huge amounts of capital in the data-center boom right now, and in AI, but a lot of it’s from private hedge funds, and a lot of it is from private capital markets. Are there ways to deal with a crash that let the people who’ve perpetrated this, like, eat the downside? And I think we really should be on—could this be an opportunity to get rid of some of the excess wealth and the inequality in this moment? We also know from the COVID pandemic that it’s possible to pop up a welfare state almost overnight. Right? The government actually can do things pretty fast when there’s a crisis. And I’ve also been thinking a lot about the Silicon Valley Bank bailout. And how that was not a, you know, critical systemic bank. And so I think—and I’m not the only one to say this. Alexis Goldstein, who is at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, and others have written about how SVB should have—maybe they should have let it fail. And so I think we should look at the past, and look at how moments like this too often have actually led to increased inequality and pernicious consequences. And just be like: How do we, if there’s a crisis moment—how do we respond? And how can we ensure that ordinary people are helped, and that the executives who perpetrated this are held accountable? Warzel: It does strike me though too that obviously the rub in that is the way that, you know, retail investing—and obviously not everyone has money in the stock market. But how much that retail investing in people’s, you know, 401(k)s and pension plans and all that are tied up in these again, these “Magnificent Seven” tech stocks. Taylor: Yeah. I just want to say the organizer in me is like: We need a mass movement that restructures retirement in America. 401(k) is a pretty recent invention. Like, why is this the mechanism through which we guarantee—and don’t guarantee, frankly, undermine—security in old age? Klein: So the point is, Social Security came out of the market crash of 1929, right? I mean, why the unfairness of that produced fairness, right? And the thing about AI—and this has been coming up for us a lot on our book tour over the last month—is: The offer of it really is only seductive, only appealing, once we’ve already destroyed and cut our social and care infrastructures to the bone, right? Like—if your kids are being taught by a teacher who’s allowed to be as great a teacher as they want to be, with relatively good student-teacher ratios? And they’re able to, you know, use their creativity and love of learning? Then the idea that they could be easily replaced with a chat bot is absurd. You know that, right? But if you’ve already cut your public education system to the bone? If you’re crowding 35 kids into a classroom. If your teacher is completely overworked and overstressed and being told that they need to teach to the test anyway. Then it’s really all just about, you know, checking boxes and a multiple-choice exam. That is something that—if you then come in and be like “Everybody can have their AI tutors,” that’s a lot more appealing, right? Or if we’re already neglecting our elders, and they’re living alone and isolated, and we’ve destroyed the infrastructure where they used to be able to hang out and have fun? Then the idea that they could be made a little bit less lonely by talking to a chatbot then becomes appealing. Right? So this will be a moment when we can decide to invest in people, infrastructure. Which is one of the things that we hear from folks who are fighting data centers in places like Memphis. Like: Why are we getting these massive data centers instead of a community center or public transit, or any of the things that we need? Right? And so there is this interplay between our neglect of the animate human physical world and the offer of AI. And that is—I think we need to go that deep in the correction of thinking about “How do we respond to this crisis?” Taylor: Yeah. And I just want to say, though: Part of what’s maddening is, as you just said, the SpaceX perspective—which is like science fiction—is somehow taken as serious in our culture. But the idea that, “Hey, we could have a different kind of retirement system, where people are taken care of in old age” seems completely absurd. But we got Social Security after the crash of 1929, after the Great Depression. But also, we only got it because old people were organized. There’s something called the Townsend movement . And like, millions and millions of old people who were broke and had no real power were like: We deserve to have an income from the government. Like: We deserve to live . And they were incredibly persistent, and they put this demand on the table that was completely unprecedented, because Social Security didn’t exist. And now we live in the world they created. So we have to be ready. This is our version of prep, right? We have to be ready with the infrastructure. And with the demands that, yeah, seem crazy today, but might just be common sense when we make it through to the other side. Warzel: So let’s talk about one of the roadblocks to that. Which is obviously the politics of all this. A defining feature, as you all have written about, as I’ve written about, of our era. And this argument that you have is that we’re living in a time of genuine elite impunity. Klein: I’m so glad. I was excited to talk to you about impunity. That was such a great essay of yours. Warzel: Here we go. This week, as we’re recording this, The New York Times has reported that Musk, world’s richest man, personally invested $366 million so far in this election cycle. It seems that Musk’s wealth, especially here in politics, is just a genuine chaos agent, right? It is very hard to exact a financial toll on him, as things are right now. And he’s able to use his money—he’s purchasing not only influence but communications infrastructure. Buying Twitter, turning it into X and this political weapon. What does the world do about this man? Taylor: So I think the first thing to do is to settle into how not okay this is, and how deeply anti-democratic this is, and how offensive it is. And then yeah—we have to organize. I mean, you know, he has had some big losses, right? Remember the whole Wisconsin Supreme Court race, where he even went like dancing around with the cheese on his head? So I think people need to show up and vote. And then we need to build a serious mass movement that’s focused on money out of politics. And I think that this is another issue that has the potential to be really bipartisan, just like the data-center movement. You know, the polling is overwhelming on this issue, but there isn’t a lot of mobilizing around it. In part because a lot of the civic infrastructure in this country is donor funded. And so, donors are not making this a key priority. But I think citizens have to. And the time is right for something that, you know, gets at that core poison in our politics. Which is wealth and power. And then, I mean, ultimately the point is—you know, we argue in the book that this really isn’t about these individual men and their pathologies and their wounded egos or whatever. It is about the wealth itself. Klein: And a belief that their wealth should buy them impunity. That the point of having hundreds of billions of dollars, or maybe a trillion dollars, is that of course the rules don’t apply. Warzel: It does seem to me—and my kind of theory, around a lot of the data-center stuff, and the fact that you see a lot of protest from each side, and this very public distaste with not only data centers but a lot of artificial-intelligence technology being foisted on people. And then having Donald Trump kind of double down on this. To me, it feels like the beginnings of a politics that doesn’t actually focus on this one guy. It feels like an opportunity. It feels like a place that, you know, where this volatility could come in. And that’s what I think is really interesting about the fact that he doesn’t seem to really—as someone who, you know, usually can ride a lot of these waves—he doesn’t seem capable of doing that. But I want to actually use that to press here on feasible solutions. And people are so mad about the incursion of AI into real communities, and the use of natural resources. Or how loud they are, or the fact that the resources in their town are going toward a data center instead of toward other infrastructure that they need. And I talked to Democratic consultants who are like. This isn’t just the issue; it’s like the issue that should just be winnable. And yet, I don’t know if there is a truly coherent politics around it. So in your minds, what is it that politics around AI need to look like going forward? Into 2028? Taylor: Yeah. I mean, I think there’s different approaches and different debates within the Democratic Party. My position is always that, you know, it’s good when people are at a place like “the polling against data centers is encouraging.” People are not fans of AI. They don’t trust the tech oligarchs. But also, you know, we as political actors need to nurture that perspective and give it shape, and expand it into something that is a broader politics, right? Like, we’re not just engaging with something that’s frozen. And so I think, you know, it is pretty inchoate. But there are people who are like, This is just a NIMBY movement. Or it’s just about, you know: People just don’t like the local data center, but maybe they actually kind of use AI when they say they don’t like it. But I think my perspective is that it’s tapping into a bigger set of anxieties. Like: What kind of future is on offer? Who makes the decisions in our world, right? Because so many of these data centers come under the cover of NDA. It’s like: What is work? What is purpose? These are really meaningful, powerful things for us to tap into. And they’re about much more than tech. We have to understand it as embedded in a broader society in social conditions. And I think with AI, we need to do the same. Like this isn’t—we can’t separate AI from this question of “how do we structure our retirements?” Right? As Naomi said: Are our schools well funded? Do our jobs pay us enough to live? This is a moment when we really need to invest in the things human beings need to live well. Like—if we need to invest in our schools, invest in health care, invest in housing, invest in human beings doing the meaningful work. And I feel like that will resonate powerfully in this moment. And then if people can deliver on that, I think it could change our politics. Right? Warzel: I find that to be a really important point in all this. I’ve been writing a lot about this moment as a crisis of agency, right? One side is this crisis of agency that’s being manufactured by Silicon Valley. Which is saying: We’re going to enact our agency to take away yours and give you these tools that do everything for you. Taylor: Mm-hmm. Warzel: But on the other side, I think there is this huge conversation of: “What is a human for?” Which is exactly what you’re saying and alluding to. And thinking of the crisis of agency as an opportunity to reopen—because we are all having, whether we believe in it or not, we’re having lots of very weird existential conversations, right? About everything. Klein: Yeah. And, you know, some of them are good, where we are. Like, I’ve seen some really beautiful conversations happening, where visual artists and musicians are really talking about what it takes to make visual art, and what it is like to do that labor, and why it matters. And I don’t think that we’ve had many spaces to like just talk about why making art matters. And what it is actually like from the artist’s perspective to do it. Or even an interesting conversation that I heard, you know, with a mathematician about what it is like to solve a math problem. And I just—I’ve never actually heard a mathematician describe it so beautifully. So I think those conversations—where we’re kind of getting back to basics about what it is that we love about what we do, and what each other does. And can we find some wonder in that and marvel in that? So that we are less susceptible to Sam Altman telling us intelligence is something that is like a utility that can be supplied? And so is art, and it’s like a vending machine and it can just spew it out, right? So, I think we’ve been—like I was saying before, the more mechanized we become, the easier it is to just let AI fill in the last step, right? Like, the more we act like robots online, the more we’re replaceable by AI bots. So we’re gonna have to become more human. Like, figure out how to become more human and irreplaceable. But yeah—I think it’s quite a spiritual moment, in a way. And a lot of people are stepping into that. Warzel: I wanna end on a point here and get your thoughts—which is that one reading of End Times Fascism , paired with the interpretation of the rightward pivot in Silicon Valley, is that a lot of people, I think, were fooled or simply unable to pay attention to what was going on. And that the tech giants and their leaders built these tools that they argued would democratize voices. That would bring people together, would expand opportunity, get rid of gatekeepers. And what they’ve done instead is create something different. This redistribution of power and control and money—all in their favor. Maybe it’s, you know, a mirror world of the techno-optimism, right? And say that the end of Trump, down the line, marks the data-center backlash. All that marks a genuine resistance to this. And say we start to get some accountability for the end-timers. We start to get, you know, steps toward regulation. How do we stop this from happening again? How do we recognize this before it’s too late? Taylor: I think this is why it’s really important to have an understanding of, and criticism of, capitalism as a system, actually. Because that is part of what got us into this mess. So, you know, I’m thinking again about the sort of era you just described, where they were promising to bring democracy through social media. And there was, I remember a piece, by Lawrence Lessig. Who is quite an influential critic of all the ways our democracy is broken. But he’s essentially saying, you know: We need to cheer on the Googles and Facebooks of the world over the old-media dinosaurs. And it was like, because they’re new, right? Because they’re new. They’re the disruptors. They’re disrupting the dinosaurs. And it was like, yeah, but they’re what is going to make them different, right? Once they disrupt the old-media ecosystem— and they are the new platforms, the new gatekeepers—why should we trust them anymore? So I think understanding the way we are in an economic system that concentrates wealth—where people are relentlessly pushed toward endless growth, right? And endless resource consumption is really critical. At one point in the book, we describe fascism as capitalism’s threat response. This is a movement of corporate and political elites to defend their power and their wealth. And I think it will do us a lot of favors to think systemically like that. Because then we can think about: What’s the scale of the solutions? Right? Like, what do we actually need to ensure that we don’t just watch another terrifying sequel? Warzel: Naomi Klein, Astor Taylor. Thank you very much for coming on Galaxy Brain . Klein: Thank you so much. Warzel: That’s it for us here. Thank you again to my guests, Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor. If you liked what you saw here, new episodes of Galaxy Brain drop every Friday. You can subscribe on The Atlantic ’s YouTube channel, or on Apple, or Spotify, or wherever it is that you get your podcasts. And if you want to support this work and the work of my fellow colleagues, you can subscribe to the publication at theatlantic.com/listener. That’s theatlantic.com/listener. items.title: Samsung annonce un partenariat avec Call of Duty®: Modern Warfare® 4
items.description: Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd. met en lumière son partenariat exclusif avec Activision, dans le cadre duquel l’entreprise est devenue le partenaire officiel de Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 pour les téléviseurs, les moniteurs, les barres de son et les enceintes Wi-Fi. Ce nouvel opus s’inscrit dans l’une des franchises de jeux de tir à la première personne (FPS) les plus populaires au monde. Cette collaboration associe l’univers de Call of Duty aux technologies d’affichage haut de gamme et aux solutions de gaming connecté de Samsung, afin d’offrir aux joueurs de nouvelles façons de profiter du jeu à l’approche de son lancement officiel. Récompensée à de nombreuses reprises et saluée par la critique, la franchise Call of Duty s’est imposée comme l’une des références incontournables de l’industrie du jeu vidéo. Ce partenariat marque une nouvelle étape dans l’engagement de Samsung à développer des expériences de jeu de nouvelle génération, à travers ses téléviseurs, moniteurs, barres de son, enceintes Wi-Fi et services de gaming connecté. « Nous sommes ravis de devenir le partenaire officiel de Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 pour les téléviseurs, les moniteurs, les barres de son et les enceintes Wi-Fi, et de permettre aux joueurs de profiter d’une expérience encore plus immersive grâce aux technologies d’affichage et audio haut de gamme de Samsung », a déclaré Hun Lee, Vice-Président exécutif de la division Visual Display (VD) de Samsung Electronics. Et d'ajouter : « Nous poursuivrons notre collaboration avec les principaux développeurs du secteur afin d’enrichir l’expérience gaming sur l’ensemble de notre gamme d’écrans». HDR10+ GAMING : une immersion renforcée et des détails visuels optimisés Samsung et Call of Duty ont collaboré pour intégrer la technologie HDR10+ GAMING à Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4. Celle-ci permet d’optimiser la précision des couleurs et des contrastes, pour offrir une expérience visuelle plus immersive, fidèle à la vision artistique des développeurs. « Les technologies d’affichage et de gaming de Samsung offrent une nouvelle dimension à l’expérience Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 », souligne Cody Neal, Responsable des partenariats chez Activision, notant que le partenariat avec Samsung « nous permet de mettre en valeur le jeu avec un niveau de netteté, une ampleur visuelle et une réactivité à la hauteur de l’intensité qui caractérise l’univers de Call of Duty » . Modern Warfare 4 prendra officiellement en charge le format super ultra-large 32:9 dès son lancement, permettant notamment aux utilisateurs des moniteurs Samsung Odyssey G9 de profiter d’un champ de vision élargi et d’une perception plus immersive de l’environnement de jeu. Samsung entend également offrir aux consommateurs du monde entier de nouvelles possibilités de découvrir Modern Warfare 4 à travers ses téléviseurs, ses moniteurs Odyssey et ses services de gaming. Samsung Gaming Hub a diffusé Call of Duty: NEXT en direct Dans le cadre de cette collaboration, les utilisateurs de Samsung Gaming Hub ont pu suivre en direct l’événement Call of Duty: NEXT, organisé le 21 août, directement depuis la plateforme. En amont de cet événement, une bannière promotionnelle dédiée à Call of Duty: NEXT avait été mise en avant sur l’écran d’accueil du Gaming Hub des téléviseurs Samsung, permettant aux utilisateurs de retrouver facilement la diffusion. Samsung a également proposé des codes d’accès anticipé à la bêta de Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 via l’application Samsung Promotion. Ces codes ont permis à certains joueurs sélectionnés de découvrir la version bêta du jeu du 21 au 25 août, avant l’ouverture de la bêta publique, qui s’est déroulée du 28 août au 1er septembre. Les informations relatives à la disponibilité des codes d’accès anticipé et aux modalités de participation avaient été mises à disposition des utilisateurs sur Samsung TV Gaming Hub. Samsung Gaming Hub centralise l’accès aux principaux services de cloud gaming, notamment Xbox Cloud Gaming, ainsi qu’à une sélection de contenus dédiés aux jeux vidéo. Cette plateforme permet aux utilisateurs de retrouver leurs services et contenus compatibles au sein d’une interface unique, sans avoir à changer d’appareil. Gamescom 2026 : Samsung Odyssey a mis à l’honneur la fluidité et la précision visuelle de Modern Warfare 4 Samsung a également présenté Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 sur son stand lors de la Gamescom 2026, qui s’est tenue du 26 au 30 août à Cologne, en Allemagne. Considéré comme l’un des plus grands rendez-vous mondiaux du jeu vidéo, cet événement rassemble chaque année joueurs, créateurs, éditeurs et acteurs technologiques de l’industrie. À cette occasion, Samsung a proposé à certains visiteurs de son stand des codes de téléchargement de Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Vault Edition sur Battle.net. Les visiteurs ont également eu l’opportunité de tester le titre en avant-première sur les moniteurs gaming haut de gamme Samsung Odyssey, avant sa sortie officielle prévue le 23 octobre 2026. Conçus pour répondre aux exigences des jeux vidéo modernes, les moniteurs Odyssey associent une qualité d’image exceptionnelle à une grande fluidité d’affichage, permettant aux joueurs de profiter aussi bien de la précision nécessaire aux sessions compétitives que de l’immersion visuelle offerte par les séquences les plus spectaculaires. À l’approche du lancement officiel de Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, cette collaboration illustre la volonté de Samsung de proposer des expériences gaming toujours plus immersives, en associant innovations technologiques, performances visuelles et connectivité. The post Samsung annonce un partenariat avec Call of Duty®: Modern Warfare® 4 appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: ‘Maybe it is designated for a cassava plantation’ – GoldStars boss criticises Debibi Presby pitch
items.description: Bibiani GoldStars head coach Petros Koukouras has expressed his displeasure over the state of the Debibi Presby Park, describing the playing surface as more suitable for cassava farming than football. His remarks came after Gold Stars suffered a 1-0 defeat to Debibi United over the weekend in their 2026/27 Ghana Premier League Matchday 7 fixture. Maxwell Agyemang scored right before the break to seal victory for the hosts, ending their three-match winless run and bringing them level with Gold Stars on seven points. The crucial victory also pushed Debibi United out of the relegation zone, as they keep working to establish themselves in the league. Speaking post-match, Koukouras vented his frustration with the quality of the pitch, arguing that its poor condition made it nearly impossible to focus on the game. “We cannot discuss football. I don’t think this is a pitch designated for football. Maybe it is designated for cassava plantation. I don’t have anything else to say,” he stated. Following the defeat, Gold Stars now turn their attention to Heart of Lions on October 25, knowing they have plenty of work ahead to get their campaign back on track. Debibi United, meanwhile, will look to build on their momentum when they travel to face Bechem United in their Matchday 8 fixture.

items.title: Gao : indignation après une agression sexuelle présumée à l’hôpital régional
items.description: L'hopital regional de Gao reagit apres l'agression sexuelle presumee d'une patiente hospitalisee en reanimation, decedee quelques heures plus tard. Le bureau syndical presente ses excuses a la famille et a la population, tandis qu'une enquete a ete ouverte par la gendarmerie. Dans la ville, l'affaire suscite indignation et incomprehension. Le bureau syndical de l'hopital regional de Gao est sorti de son silence. Il reconnaît les faits rapportes, presente ses condoleances a la famille de la victime et lui adresse ses excuses, ainsi qu'a l'ensemble de la population. Selon Boubacar Issa Toure, porte-parole du syndicat de l'etablissement, le suspect presume serait un ancien stagiaire qui ne fait pas partie du personnel de l'hopital. Il serait actuellement en fuite. La gendarmerie a ouvert une enquete afin de faire la lumiere sur cette affaire. Le syndicat affirme etre en contact avec la famille de la victime. Face a l'emotion suscitee par les faits rapportes, il appelle egalement la population a continuer de faire confiance au personnel soignant de l'etablissement. a Gao, des habitants reclament des responsabilites Pres de 48 heures apres l'agression sexuelle presumee, plusieurs habitants expriment leur indignation et demandent que les responsabilites soient etablies. Pour un habitant, un tel acte dans un etablissement hospitalier pourrait reveler un defaut de surveillance. « Seule la negligence peut expliquer que quelqu'un puisse rentrer a l'hopital et commettre cet acte-la. C'est meme impensable », estime-t-il. Un autre interlocuteur insiste sur la sensibilite du lieu ou les faits se seraient produits. « Surtout a un endroit tres sensible qu'est la salle de reanimation. Je dis que c'est un acte ignoble. L'etat doit vraiment prendre des precautions », declare-t-il, appelant a renforcer les mesures de securite. L'emotion est egalement vive chez un autre habitant, qui evoque un malaise plus large face aux evenements recents dans la region. « On a le cœur serre, on a le choc. Moi, ce n'est pas l'acte, en fait, qui doit interpeller la societe. C'est une succession de fautes. C'est une succession d'evenements auxquels nous assistons ces derniers temps dans la region de Gao », deplore-t-il. Pour un chef de famille interroge sur l'affaire dans la ville de Gao, la priorite est que le suspect presume soit retrouve et traduit en justice. Une enquete pour etablir les faits Pour rappel , la patiente avait ete admise en reanimation apres une intervention chirurgicale. Elle est decedee mercredi dernier, vers 14 heures, quelques heures apres l'agression sexuelle presumee. a ce stade, aucun lien n'a ete etabli entre les faits rapportes et le deces de la patiente. L'enquete ouverte par la gendarmerie devra notamment contribuer a etablir les circonstances de l'agression presumee et a determiner les eventuelles responsabilites. Lire aussi : a Gao, la consommation de drogues inquiete les familles et les professionnels de sante L’article Gao : indignation après une agression sexuelle présumée à l’hôpital régional est apparu en premier sur Studio Tamani - Informations, débats, magazines : toute l’actualité du Mali, en 5 langues .
